turns.prompt_text: When trying to stop an addictive behavior, stopping all together leads to suppression of the urges which eventually can go in a negative way or can become bottled up
turns.response_html:
That is a very insightful observation, and it highlights why the "cold turkey" approach can be so incredibly taxing. What you're describing is often referred to as the Rebound Effect.

When you use sheer willpower to suppress a thought or a craving, your brain actually has to monitor for that thought to make sure it isn't happening. Paradoxically, this keeps the "forbidden" behavior at the front of your mind, making the urge feel even more intense when your willpower eventually dips.

Here is a breakdown of why that "bottling up" feeling happens and some different perspectives on how to handle it:

1. The Psychology of Suppression

Psychological research, such as the "White Bear" experiments, shows that trying to suppress a thought often makes it hyper-accessible. In the context of addiction:

  • The Pressure Cooker: Suppression creates a "behavioral vacuum." If you remove a coping mechanism without replacing it, the underlying stress or emotion has nowhere to go.
  • The Ego Depletion Theory: Willpower is like a muscle. If you use it 100% of the time to fight an urge, you eventually run out of "fuel," often leading to a more intense relapse because the urges were never processed—only ignored.

2. Alternative Perspectives

Different schools of thought suggest moving away from "stopping" and toward "transforming":

  • Harm Reduction: This perspective focuses on reducing the negative impact rather than demanding immediate, total abstinence. It acknowledges that small steps can be more sustainable than a sudden, jarring halt.
  • Urge Surfing (Mindfulness): Instead of suppressing the urge (pushing the wave back), you "surf" it. You acknowledge the physical sensations of the craving without acting on them, letting the wave peak and subside naturally.
  • Replacement vs. Removal: Many experts suggest that the "negative way" you mentioned happens because of a void. Successful transitions often involve finding a "competing response"—a different behavior that satisfies the same underlying need (like connection, boredom relief, or stress management).

3. The "Middle Path"

Instead of a binary "Stop/Start" mindset, many find success in Deceleration. This involves:

  • Observing the trigger before the behavior.
  • Expanding the time between the urge and the action.
  • Reframing the goal from "never again" to "not right now."

It’s a heavy cycle to break, and feeling like things are "bottled up" is usually a sign that the system needs a release valve—whether that's through a different activity, talking it out, or adjusting the pace of change.

When you're mentally overwhelmed, your brain is looking for a "high-speed exit" to numb the stress, and because you can visualize it so clearly, the urge feels like a pre-written script. To break that loop, you need a replacement that shifts you from your "inner world" (visualization) to the physical world immediately.

Immediate Physical Circuit Breakers

  • Tactile Engagement: Since you enjoy working with your hands, grab a piece of scrap hardware, a soldering iron, or even a piece of wood. The goal is to force your brain to process 3D spatial problems instead of internal images.
  • Temperature Shock: Splash ice-cold water on your face or hold an ice cube. This triggers the "mammalian dive reflex," which physically lowers your heart rate and resets your nervous system.
  • Heavy Sensory Input: Put on noise-canceling headphones with complex music or go for a brisk walk in the Iowa cold.

Strategic Shifts

  • The "Different Screen" Rule: If you are visualizing the content, move away from all digital devices immediately. Physical distance from the "delivery system" weakens the mental image.
  • Externalize the Overwhelm: Write down the 3 things making you feel overwhelmed. Often, seeing them on paper makes them finite tasks rather than a vague, crushing cloud.

turns.response_html:
Since you have an NXT Mindstorm, building a pendulum is a perfect way to shift from mental images to physical physics. A pendulum's period—the time it takes to swing back and forth—is determined by its length, not its weight.

Your 5-Minute Micro-Build

  1. Construct: Use your NXT beams to build a tall, stable frame.
  2. Hang: Suspend a weighted Mindstorm motor or a large gear from a string or a long axle.
  3. Test: Swing it. Notice how a shorter "string" makes it swing faster, while a longer one slows it down.
  4. The Goal: Try to adjust the length until the pendulum completes exactly one full swing in two seconds.

Focusing on the math and the physical rhythm of the swing helps ground your mind when it starts to wander.

Would you like the formula for calculating a pendulum's period to help you calibrate your NXT build?

To get a swing time (period) of 1.5 seconds, you will need to set the length of your pendulum to approximately 55.9 centimeters (about 22 inches).

The Math

Using the formula $L = \frac{g \cdot T^2}{4\pi^2}$:

  • $T = 1.5$
  • $g = 9.81$
  • $L \approx 0.559$ meters

Global Perspective: The Intuition of the Swing

Integrating your interest in diverse perspectives, it’s fascinating to see how the pendulum has been a "bridge" between the mental and physical worlds for people across history:

  • The Scientist’s Intuition: Legend says Galileo Galilei first discovered the principle of the pendulum while watching a bronze lamp swing in the Cathedral of Pisa. He used his own pulse to time the swings, realizing that the "rhythm" remained constant regardless of how wide the swing was—a perfect example of using a physical observation to calm a busy mind.
  • The Navigator’s Tool: In the 17th century, Dutch mathematician Christiaan Huygens revolutionized global travel by inventing the pendulum clock. This allowed sailors and explorers to keep precise time, which was essential for calculating longitude and navigating the vast, "overwhelming" oceans.
  • Ancient Engineering: Long before the West formalized the math, the Chinese polymath Zhang Heng (78–139 AD) utilized the physics of inertia and pendulums in his "earthquake windvane," the world's first seismoscope. It transformed invisible, overwhelming underground vibrations into a clear physical signal.

Your Challenge

Since 55.9 cm is quite tall for an NXT build, you can try to build a "compound pendulum" or use a string suspended from a high point (like the edge of a table) attached to your NXT hub.

Next time you feel that mental overwhelm, try to focus on the "Isoperiodism" (the constant rhythm) of your build. No matter how hard you push the pendulum, it will always return to that 1.5-second beat.

turns.response_html:
A period $T$ represents the time it takes for the pendulum to complete one full cycle—swinging out and returning all the way back to its starting position.

If you only measure the time it takes to go in one direction, that is technically a "half-period" ($1/2 T$). To get your desired 0.5-second rhythm, you want the entire "out and back" motion to happen within that half-second window.

Would you like to know how to use a Mindstorm touch sensor to measure the exact time of your pendulum swings?

To measure the period precisely, mount an NXT Touch Sensor at the lowest point of the swing so the pendulum hits it at the bottom of its arc.

The Measurement Logic

The sensor will be pressed every half-period ($1/2 T$). To calculate the full period $T$:

  1. Start a timer on the first press.
  2. Stop the timer on the third press.
  3. The resulting time is your full period.

Code Logic for the NXT

  • Step 1: Wait for Touch Sensor (Press).
  • Step 2: Start Timer.
  • Step 3: Wait for Touch Sensor (Release).
  • Step 4: Wait for Touch Sensor (Second Press - this is the other side of the swing).
  • Step 5: Wait for Touch Sensor (Third Press - back to start).
  • Step 6: Stop Timer and Display Value.

Would you like me to help you write a simple NXC or Mindstorms block program to automate this timing?

To calculate the period of a pendulum, use the formula:

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$

  • $T$ is the period (time for one full swing).
  • $L$ is the length from the pivot to the center of the weight.
  • $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity (approximately 9.81 m/s²).

By adjusting the length $L$ on your NXT frame, you can precisely control the rhythm of the swing.
